title: Switch expressions
hook: Auth token kind is a value. A switch expression returns a pipeline; a switch statement is for when you must sequence side effects.

sections.heading: Arms, discards, and exhaustiveness
sections.prose: A switch expression selects the first matching arm and produces a value. Arms use patterns, not case labels. There is no fall-through. The compiler warns when the input type is not fully covered and when an arm is subsumed by an earlier one. _ matches whatever remains; omitting it on a non-exhaustive input makes the compiler complain, and at run time an unmatched value throws. Enum switches should still have _ because an enum can hold an undefined integer.

snippets.label: Token kind to a processing mode
snippets.explanation: Each arm is a value. The discard is a hard failure, not AuthMode.Oidc. That default-to-privileged-path bug is an interview favorite.

sections.heading: Switch statement still exists
sections.prose: Use a switch statement when arms must contain multiple statements without wrapping them in local functions, or when you are matching in a void method. You can mix pattern case labels (case AuthToken { Scheme: "LTI" } t:) with when guards. Do not convert a statement to an expression by stuffing side effects into a discarded value. Readability beats uniformity.

snippets.label: Pattern case in a switch statement
snippets.explanation: when is a guard evaluated after the pattern matches. The property pattern avoids a nest of ifs on Scheme and Version.

interviewTakeaways: Switch expressions return a value and must be exhaustive (or use _).
First matching arm wins; order is part of the spec.
Enums are not closed at run time; keep a discard.
Throw on unknown auth schemes; never fall through to the privileged mode.
commonPitfalls: Using _ => 0 as a silent default for token TTL or role.
Overlapping relational arms in the wrong order so a later arm never runs.
Expecting fall-through like C or older JS switch.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS switch falls through without break. C# switch statements do not (except empty cases). C# switch expressions cannot fall through at all. JS has no exhaustiveness checker unless you use a never helper in TypeScript.
TS switch on a union tag plus never in default is the analogue of C# exhaustive switch expressions on records or enums.
